title: Clinical Risk Assessment in Periodontal Disease — Test

mcqs.q: Disease risk is defined as:
opts: The probability that an individual will develop a specific disease in a given period
The proportion of a population already affected by a disease
The severity of disease once it has developed
The rate at which an existing disease progresses
mcqs.explain: It is a probability that varies from individual to individual, not a measure of existing disease.

mcqs.q: Risk factors are best described as:
opts: Environmental, behavioral or biologic factors that increase the likelihood of developing the disease
Findings that always accompany established disease
Unmodifiable characteristics present from birth
Factors identified only in cross-sectional studies
mcqs.explain: Unmodifiable characteristics are risk determinants, and cross-sectional-only findings are risk indicators.

mcqs.q: For an exposure to be identified as a RISK FACTOR, it must occur:
opts: Before disease onset
At the same time as disease onset
After disease onset
At any time, provided it is statistically associated
mcqs.explain: Temporality is the criterion that separates a true risk factor from a mere association.

mcqs.q: Exposure to a risk factor may occur:
opts: At a single point in time, over multiple separate points, or continuously
Only continuously throughout life
Only at a single defined point in time
Only during childhood
mcqs.explain: All three exposure patterns qualify, which is why history-taking must cover past as well as present exposures.

mcqs.q: A risk DETERMINANT (background characteristic) is:
opts: A risk factor that cannot be modified
A factor confirmed only in cross-sectional studies
A factor associated with disease that does not cause it
A factor that always precedes disease onset
mcqs.explain: Age, gender and genetic factors are examples — they cannot be changed by intervention.

mcqs.q: Risk INDICATORS are:
opts: Putative factors from cross-sectional studies, not confirmed longitudinally
Risk factors that cannot be modified by the patient
Findings associated with disease that do not cause it
Factors proven causal in randomised intervention trials
mcqs.explain: They are candidate risk factors awaiting longitudinal confirmation — HIV/AIDS, osteoporosis and infrequent dental visits are the examples given.

mcqs.q: Risk PREDICTORS (markers) are characterised by the fact that they:
opts: Are associated with increased risk for disease, but do not cause the disease
Cannot be modified by treatment
Have been confirmed causal in longitudinal studies
Only appear after the disease has resolved
mcqs.explain: Previous history of periodontal disease and bleeding on probing are markers of risk rather than causes of it.

mcqs.q: Which of the following is classified as a risk DETERMINANT rather than a risk factor?
opts: Age
Tobacco smoking
Diabetes mellitus
Pathogenic bacteria
mcqs.explain: The other three can all be modified or treated; age cannot.

mcqs.q: The relationship between smoking and the prevalence of periodontal disease is:
opts: Direct, and independent of other factors
Present only in patients who also have diabetes
Confined to patients over 60 years of age
Inverse in former smokers
mcqs.explain: Smoking is a well-established risk factor and also has a negative impact on the response to therapy.

mcqs.q: An important variable in the relationship between diabetes mellitus and periodontitis is:
opts: The level of diabetic control
The duration of the patient's dental treatment
Whether the patient wears a prosthesis
The patient's gender
mcqs.explain: Prevalence and severity are higher in both type 1 and type 2 diabetes, and glycaemic control modulates that effect.

mcqs.q: The relationship between plaque accumulation and gingivitis is described as:
opts: Causal — gingivitis can be reversed with good oral hygiene measures
Merely an association with no causal basis
Causal only in diabetic patients
Present only when calculus is also present
mcqs.explain: The reversibility on removing the plaque is what establishes the causal relationship.

mcqs.q: Patients with severe loss of attachment often have minimal levels of bacterial plaque. This indicates that:
opts: The quality of the plaque biofilm is important, not only its quantity
Plaque plays no role in periodontitis
Plaque indices are unreliable measures
Attachment loss is purely genetic in these patients
mcqs.explain: This is why specific pathogenic species, rather than bulk plaque, are named as risk factors.

mcqs.q: Which three bacteria are named as risk factors for periodontal disease?
opts: Aggregatibacter actinomycetemcomitans, Porphyromonas gingivalis and Tannerella forsythia
Streptococcus mutans, Lactobacillus acidophilus and Actinomyces viscosus
Streptococcus sanguinis, Veillonella parvula and Neisseria species
Candida albicans, Streptococcus mitis and Fusobacterium nucleatum
mcqs.explain: The first option lists the red-complex-associated organisms implicated in periodontal destruction, not the cariogenic or early-colonising species.

mcqs.q: The shift from periodontal health to disease is a shift from:
opts: Symbiotic to dysbiotic microorganisms
Anaerobic to aerobic microorganisms
Gram-negative to Gram-positive microorganisms
Motile to non-motile microorganisms
mcqs.explain: Dysbiosis describes a community whose composition has shifted away from one compatible with health.

mcqs.q: The keystone pathogen that induces the dysbiotic shift is:
opts: Porphyromonas gingivalis
Aggregatibacter actinomycetemcomitans
Tannerella forsythia
Treponema denticola
mcqs.explain: A keystone pathogen can remodel the whole community even when present in low numbers.

mcqs.q: Which of the following are described as ANATOMIC factors harbouring plaque?
opts: Furcations, root concavities and developmental grooves
Overhanging restoration margins
Subgingival crown margins
Supragingival calculus ledges
mcqs.explain: Overhangs and subgingival margins are restorative factors; calculus is considered separately as a plaque reservoir.

mcqs.q: Subgingival and overhanging margins in restorations lead to:
opts: Increased plaque accumulation, increased inflammation and increased bone loss
Increased plaque accumulation only, with no tissue consequence
Reduced plaque retention because of their smooth surface
Increased bone loss without any increase in inflammation
mcqs.explain: All three consequences follow, which is why margin placement is a periodontal as well as a restorative decision.

mcqs.q: Calculus is regarded as a risk factor for periodontitis because it:
opts: Acts as a reservoir of bacterial plaque
Is itself directly toxic to the periodontal ligament
Prevents the gingiva from adapting to the tooth
Chemically dissolves the alveolar bone
mcqs.explain: Its mineralised surface is always covered by a layer of unmineralised, living plaque.

mcqs.q: Alterations in which gene are associated with severe periodontitis?
opts: The genes encoding interleukin-1
The genes encoding interleukin-10
The genes encoding collagen type I
The genes encoding amelogenin
mcqs.explain: IL-1 genotype-positive status is also marked on the systemic vector of the risk assessment diagram.

mcqs.q: Studies showing minimal loss of attachment in aging subjects enrolled in preventive programs demonstrate that:
opts: Periodontal disease is not an inevitable consequence of the aging process
Age is not associated with periodontal disease at all
Preventive programs are only effective in young patients
Attachment loss is entirely genetically determined
mcqs.explain: Prevalence rises with age because of cumulative exposure, not because aging itself must destroy the periodontium.

mcqs.q: Why may loss of attachment have more consequences in YOUNGER patients?
opts: Longer exposure to causative factors, so greater risk of disease as they age
Their periodontal tissues heal considerably more slowly
They have significantly thinner alveolar bone
They are less likely to harbour pathogenic bacteria
mcqs.explain: The same amount of loss at a young age signals a steeper lifetime trajectory of destruction.

mcqs.q: Gender differences in attachment loss appear to be related to:
opts: Preventive practices rather than any genetic factor
Hormonal differences between the sexes
Differences in salivary flow rate
Differences in alveolar bone density
mcqs.explain: Men have more attachment loss and poorer oral hygiene than women, which points to behaviour rather than biology.

mcqs.q: Gingivitis and poor oral hygiene related to lower socioeconomic status are attributed to:
opts: Decreased dental awareness and decreased frequency of dental visits
A genetically determined immune deficiency
A higher prevalence of diabetes in that group
Increased consumption of fermentable carbohydrate
mcqs.explain: The mechanism is access to and uptake of care, not an inherent biological difference.

mcqs.q: Emotional stress may affect the periodontium by:
opts: Interfering with normal immune function and increasing levels of circulating hormones
Directly increasing the virulence of P. gingivalis
Reducing salivary buffering capacity alone
Causing resorption of the alveolar crest directly
mcqs.explain: Bereavement, divorce, financial strain, distress and depression are the stressful life events cited.

mcqs.q: Osteoporosis is classified as a risk INDICATOR because it:
opts: Does not initiate periodontitis, though reduced bone mass may aggravate disease progression
Is a proven cause of attachment loss
Cannot be modified by any treatment
Occurs only after periodontal disease is established
mcqs.explain: It modifies the course of existing disease rather than starting it.

mcqs.q: The status of infrequent dental visits as a risk factor is described as:
opts: Controversial, requiring additional longitudinal and intervention studies
Firmly established by longitudinal studies
Disproven by intervention studies
Relevant only in patients with diabetes
mcqs.explain: This is precisely why it sits among the risk indicators rather than the risk factors.

mcqs.q: The best clinical indicator of gingival inflammation is:
opts: Bleeding on probing
Probing depth
Radiographic bone level
Tooth mobility
mcqs.explain: BOP is an objective inflammatory parameter that can be recorded at every site.

mcqs.q: An EXCELLENT predictor of future loss of attachment is:
opts: Bleeding on probing coupled with increasing pocket depth
Bleeding on probing alone in shallow sites
Probing depth alone with no bleeding
The number of restorations present
mcqs.explain: Either sign alone is weaker; it is the combination that predicts future breakdown.

mcqs.q: Lack of bleeding on probing is:
opts: An excellent indicator of periodontal health
A sign that the probe force was too light to be diagnostic
Meaningless in a maintenance patient
Found only in patients who have never had periodontitis
mcqs.explain: The negative predictive value of absent bleeding is its greatest clinical strength.

mcqs.q: Which patients are at the GREATEST risk for future loss of attachment?
opts: Those with the most severe existing loss of attachment
Those with the greatest number of restorations
Those who have never attended for maintenance
Those with the highest plaque scores
mcqs.explain: A history of previous periodontal disease is a good clinical predictor of risk for future disease.

mcqs.q: The American Academy of Periodontology recommends that risk assessment be:
opts: Part of all comprehensive and all periodic periodontal evaluations
Reserved for patients who have already lost attachment
Performed once only, at the very first visit
Used only in research, not in clinical settings
mcqs.explain: Previously identified risk elements are also to be reassessed at the re-evaluation stage.

mcqs.q: How many parameters form the basis of the Lang and Tonetti periodontal risk assessment?
opts: Six
Four
Five
Eight
mcqs.explain: BOP %, pockets ≥ 5 mm, tooth loss, bone loss/age, systemic factors and environmental factors.

mcqs.q: On the functional diagram, LOW risk corresponds to a position:
opts: Within the centre circle of the polygon
Between the two rings in bold
Outside the periphery of the second bold ring
On the outermost tip of the vector
mcqs.explain: Moderate risk lies between the two bold rings, and high risk outside the second bold ring.

mcqs.q: The divisions marked on the BOP vector are:
mcqs.explain: The 2–12 linear scale belongs to the pocket-count and tooth-loss vectors; the 0.25 increments belong to BL/Age.

mcqs.q: For bleeding on probing, HIGH risk for re-infection is indicated by a value:
opts: Greater than 25 %
Greater than 10 %
Greater than 49 %
Greater than 16 %
mcqs.explain: Below 10 % is low risk; the > 49 % mark is simply the outermost division on the vector.

mcqs.q: Regarding residual pockets ≥ 5 mm, LOW risk is indicated by:
opts: Up to 4 residual pockets
Up to 8 residual pockets
Up to 12 residual pockets
Up to 2 residual pockets
mcqs.explain: More than 8 residual pockets indicates high risk for recurrent disease.

mcqs.q: Tooth loss is counted out of a total of how many teeth?
mcqs.explain: The third molars are excluded from the count.

mcqs.q: More than how many teeth lost places the patient in the HIGH-risk band?
mcqs.explain: Up to 4 teeth lost is low risk; the scale runs 2, 4, 6, 8, 10 and ≥ 12.

mcqs.q: When estimating bone loss from radiographs, which site provides the value?
opts: The site with the greatest loss
The mean of all posterior sites
The site adjacent to the deepest pocket
The first molar region on the right side
mcqs.explain: The worst site defines the patient's bone loss value for this vector.

mcqs.q: One millimeter of bone loss equates to what percentage of bone loss?
mcqs.explain: The resulting percentage is then divided by the patient's age to give the BL/Age factor.

mcqs.q: On the BL/Age vector, the division between MODERATE and HIGH risk is at:
mcqs.explain: 0.5 separates low from moderate; the scale runs in increments of 0.25.

mcqs.q: A 40-year-old patient whose worst site shows 4 mm of bone loss has a BL/Age factor of:
opts: 1.0 — the division between moderate and high risk
0.4 — low risk
4.0 — far into the high-risk zone
0.1 — low risk
mcqs.explain: 4 mm equals 40 % bone loss, and 40 ÷ 40 = 1.0.

mcqs.q: The systemic vector is marked in the HIGH-risk area in patients with:
opts: Type I or type II diabetes mellitus and IL-1 genotype positive patients
Any history of antibiotic use
Osteoporosis alone
A family history of tooth loss
mcqs.explain: These are the systemic conditions linked to disease susceptibility and progression on this vector.

mcqs.q: On the environmental vector, HEAVY smokers are defined as consuming:
opts: ≥ 20 cigarettes per day
≥ 10 cigarettes per day
≥ 15 cigarettes per day
≥ 30 cigarettes per day
mcqs.explain: Occasional is < 10/day and moderate is 10–19/day — both of which fall in the moderate-risk band.

mcqs.q: Which smoking group is classified as LOW risk for recurrence?
opts: Non-smokers and former smokers
Occasional smokers only
Occasional and moderate smokers
Former smokers only
mcqs.explain: Former smokers return to the low-risk band, which is a powerful motivational message for the patient.

mcqs.q: A LOW PRA patient is defined as one who has:
opts: All parameters in the low-risk categories, or at most one parameter in the moderate-risk category
At most two parameters in the moderate-risk category
No parameter in the high-risk category, regardless of the moderate ones
All six parameters strictly within the centre circle
mcqs.explain: One moderate parameter is still permitted within the low grade.

mcqs.q: A MODERATE PRA patient has:
opts: At least two parameters in the moderate category, but at most one in the high-risk category
At least two parameters in the high-risk category
Exactly three parameters in the moderate category
One parameter in the moderate category and none high
mcqs.explain: Once a second parameter reaches the high-risk band the patient becomes high PRA.

mcqs.q: A HIGH PRA patient has:
opts: At least two parameters in the high-risk category
At least one parameter in the high-risk category
All six parameters in the moderate category
At least four parameters in the moderate category
mcqs.explain: A single high parameter is still compatible with a moderate overall grade.

mcqs.q: In Fig 2, the low-risk maintenance patient had which BOP value?
mcqs.explain: The same patient had 4 residual pockets ≥ 5 mm, 2 teeth lost, a BL/Age factor of 0.25, no systemic factor and was a non-smoker.

saqs.q: Define risk factor, risk determinant, risk indicator and risk predictor, and give one example of each.
saqs.a: RISK FACTOR — environmental, behavioral or biologic, increasing likelihood of disease, exposure preceding onset (tobacco smoking). RISK DETERMINANT — a risk factor that cannot be modified (age, gender, genetics). RISK INDICATOR — probable factor from cross-sectional but not longitudinal studies (HIV/AIDS, osteoporosis). RISK PREDICTOR/MARKER — associated with risk but not causal (bleeding on probing, previous periodontal disease).

head: Term
Definition
Example
rows: environmental, behavioral or biologic factor that increases the likelihood of disease; exposure must occur before onset
a risk factor that cannot be modified
probable or putative factor from cross-sectional studies, not confirmed longitudinally
associated with increased risk but does not cause the disease
bleeding on probing, previous history of periodontal disease

saqs.q: List the risk FACTORS for periodontal disease and summarise the role of each.
saqs.a: TOBACCO SMOKING — well established, a direct relationship independent of other factors, with a negative impact on response to therapy. DIABETES MELLITUS — clear risk factor; higher prevalence and severity in types 1 and 2, with the level of control an important variable. PATHOGENIC BACTERIA AND DEPOSITS — plaque causes gingivitis (causal, reversible); quality matters as well as quantity; A. actinomycetemcomitans, P. gingivalis and T. forsythia are the three identified.

head: Risk factor
Role

a clear risk factor — prevalence and severity higher in type 1 and type 2, and the level of control is an important variable

plaque accumulation causes gingivitis — a causal, reversible relationship. Quality of the biofilm matters as well as quantity; the three bacteria identified are A. actinomycetemcomitans, P. gingivalis and T. forsythia

saqs.q: Explain the concept of dysbiosis and the keystone pathogen in periodontal disease.
saqs.a: The transition from health to disease is a shift from SYMBIOTIC to DYSBIOTIC microorganisms — the community changes from one compatible with health to one that drives destruction. P. gingivalis is the KEYSTONE PATHOGEN: it induces the shift, remodelling the community even though it is not necessarily the most numerous organism.

P. gingivalis — it induces the shift, remodelling the community even though it is not necessarily the most numerous organism present

saqs.q: Name the anatomic and restorative local factors that increase periodontal risk, and explain why calculus is included.
saqs.a: ANATOMIC — furcations, root concavities, developmental grooves; they harbor plaque and challenge instrumentation. RESTORATIVE — subgingival and overhanging margins, giving more plaque, more inflammation and more bone loss. CALCULUS is included because it acts as a RESERVOIR of bacterial plaque.

head: Factor
Why it increases risk
rows: furcations, root concavities, developmental grooves — they harbor bacterial plaque and present a challenge during instrumentation
subgingival and overhanging margins — increased plaque accumulation, increased inflammation and increased bone loss
acts as a reservoir of bacterial plaque

saqs.q: List the five risk determinants/background characteristics for periodontal disease.
saqs.a: Genetic factors · age · gender · socioeconomic status · stress.

list: Genetic factors
Age
Gender
Socioeconomic status
Stress

saqs.q: Discuss age as a risk determinant for periodontal disease.
saqs.a: Prevalence and severity increase with age, and degenerative changes may increase susceptibility. But attachment and bone loss result from PROLONGED EXPOSURE to other risk factors — a cumulative effect. Subjects in preventive programs show minimal loss, so periodontal disease is NOT an inevitable consequence of aging. Loss in younger patients matters more, as they have longer exposure ahead and so greater risk of continued disease.

list: Prevalence and severity increase with age, and degenerative changes of aging may increase susceptibility
But attachment and bone loss result from prolonged exposure to other risk factors over a lifetime — a cumulative effect
Subjects in preventive programs show minimal loss, so periodontal disease is NOT an inevitable consequence of aging
Loss of attachment matters more in younger patients — a longer time for exposure ahead, and so greater risk of continued disease as they age

saqs.q: Name the three risk INDICATORS for periodontal disease and state the status of each.
saqs.a: HIV/AIDS — immune dysfunction increases susceptibility, though good oral health measures can maintain health. OSTEOPOROSIS — does not initiate periodontitis, but reduced bone mass may aggravate progression. INFREQUENT DENTAL VISITS — controversial; more longitudinal and intervention studies are needed.

head: Indicator
Status
rows: the associated immune dysfunction increases susceptibility — though patients practising good oral health measures can maintain periodontal health
does not initiate periodontitis, but the reduced bone mass may aggravate progression
controversial as a risk factor — additional longitudinal and intervention studies are necessary

saqs.q: List the six parameters that form the basis of the periodontal risk assessment for supportive periodontal therapy.
saqs.a: % bleeding on probing · number of pockets ≥5 mm · teeth lost of 28 · % bone loss relative to age · systemic factors · environmental factors.

list: Percentage of bleeding on probing
Number of pockets with probing depth ≥ 5 mm
Loss of teeth from a total of 28
Percentage of bone loss relative to age
Systemic factors
Environmental factors

saqs.q: Explain how the functional (spider web) diagram is read.
saqs.a: Each vector is one risk factor, divided into low, moderate and high risk. LOW lies within the centre circle; MODERATE between the two bold rings; HIGH outside the second bold ring. Plotting all six creates a polygon whose shape shows the overall risk of progression.

head: Zone
Where
rows: within the centre circle of the polygon
outside the periphery of the second bold ring

ans.text: Each vector represents one risk factor or indicator. Plotting all six parameters creates a polygon whose shape shows the overall risk for disease progression.

saqs.q: State the low- and high-risk cut-offs for bleeding on probing, residual pockets and tooth loss.
saqs.a: BOP — <10% low, >25% high; divisions 4, 9, 16, 25, 36, >49%. RESIDUAL POCKETS ≥5 mm — up to 4 low, more than 8 high; scale 2, 4, 6, 8, 10, ≥12. TOOTH LOSS of 28 — up to 4 low, more than 8 high; same scale.

saqs.q: Describe how the bone loss / age factor is calculated and interpreted.
saqs.a: Estimate % bone loss from posterior radiographs, the worst site giving the value; 1 mm = 10% bone loss. Divide the percentage by the patient's age. The scale runs in increments of 0.25 of BL/Age — 0.5 divides low from moderate, 1.0 divides moderate from high.

list: Estimate the percentage of bone loss from radiographs of the posterior teeth — the site with the greatest loss gives the value
1 mm = 10% bone loss
Divide the percentage by the patient's age
The scale runs in increments of 0.25 of the factor BL/Age — 0.5 divides low from moderate, 1.0 divides moderate from high

saqs.q: Define a low, moderate and high PRA patient.
saqs.a: LOW — all parameters low risk, or at most one moderate. MODERATE — at least two moderate, but at most one high. HIGH — at least two parameters high risk.

head: PRA
Definition
rows: all parameters in the low-risk categories, or at most one in the moderate category
at least two parameters moderate, but at most one in the high-risk category
at least two parameters in the high-risk category

saqs.q: State the smoking categories used on the environmental vector and the risk band assigned to each.
saqs.a: Non-smokers and former smokers — LOW risk. Occasional (<10/day) and moderate (10–19/day) — MODERATE risk. Heavy (≥20/day) — the HIGHER risk group.

saqs.q: Summarise the clinical purpose of periodontal risk assessment.
saqs.a: Risk assessment identifies elements that predispose to periodontal disease or influence progression of existing disease; such patients may need their prognosis and treatment plan modified. Patients should be educated about their risk — a smoker informed of the link with periodontitis — and intervention strategies implemented where appropriate. Previously identified risk elements must be REASSESSED at re-evaluation.
